title: English Vocabulary 4 · Units 69–70
description: Advanced C1–C2 vocabulary for difficult situations, idiomatic reactions, modal interpretations, degrees of probability, obligations and expressions of desire.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-supplied source. Vocabulary targets and distinctions follow the teaching units, exercises and answer key; Portuguese translations, examples and explanatory notes are independently written. Original exercises, long passages, tables and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Units 69 and 70 teaching pages, adjective and collocation tables, language notes, exercises 69.1–69.4 and 70.1–70.5, and corresponding answer-key entries.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA for short items where confident. Longer phrases and entries with uncertain connected speech have empty IPA rather than speculative transcriptions.
audit.languagePolicy: All titles, objectives, examples, notes and metadata are in English; Brazilian Portuguese is restricted to the pt field.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared the teaching pages and exercises with the relevant answer key; reviewed word senses, prepositions, connotations and register; independently wrote examples and usage notes; checked the JSON against the canonical keys and inspected word-audio targets for unsuitable grammar markup.
audit.limitations: No MP3 files are included. Live VocabLab import, browser TTS pronunciation and speech recognition were not tested.

units.title: Unit 69 — Difficulties and dilemmas
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 69. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Basic concepts · difficulties, obstacles and register
learningObjectives: Differentiate small snags and hitches from substantial setbacks, obstacles and ordeals.
Choose adjectives for mental complexity, physical effort, distress and deliberate obstruction.
Use informal difficulty idioms with accurate grammar, register and prepositions.
Use the singular noun difficulty naturally in the pattern have difficulty (in) doing something.

items.example: The main snag is that the laboratory is unavailable on Fridays.
items.note: A relatively minor obstacle or inconvenient detail; usually more general than glitch.

items.example: The launch went ahead despite a minor hitch in the schedule.
items.note: A small, often temporary problem that interrupts a plan.

items.example: A software glitch caused the display to freeze during the demonstration.
items.note: Especially a minor technical malfunction, unlike the more general hitch or snag.

items.example: Losing the prototype was a serious setback for the research team.
items.note: An event that delays or reverses progress, rather than a small inconvenience.

items.pt: obstáculo que impede o avanço; entrave
items.example: Securing ethical approval became the main stumbling block in the study.
items.note: An issue that prevents further progress, especially negotiations or plans.

items.example: One pitfall of remote measurements is relying on an unstable network connection.
items.note: An often hidden or unexpected problem; frequently plural in advice about risks.

items.example: Limited funding remains an obstacle to expanding the programme.
items.note: Something that blocks movement or progress, literally or figuratively.

items.pt: impedimento; fator que dificulta o progresso
items.example: Poor accessibility is a major impediment to participation.
items.note: A formal term for something that restricts free action, progress or movement.

items.example: She faced a dilemma between accepting a promotion and staying near her family.
items.note: A difficult choice, often between two options with significant disadvantages.

items.example: The twelve-hour rescue was an exhausting ordeal for everyone involved.
items.note: A severe, distressing or physically demanding experience, not merely a decision.

items.example: The proposal is problematic because it depends on unverified assumptions.
items.note: Describes something that raises a range of difficulties or concerns.

items.example: The philosopher's argument was too abstruse for an introductory lecture.
items.note: Applied to intellectually demanding theories or ideas, rather than physically hard work.

items.example: Calibrating each instrument by hand was an arduous task.
items.note: Emphasises sustained effort and fatigue in a task or journey.

items.example: The system is complex because several subsystems must be synchronised.
items.note: Difficulty comes from having many interconnected components, not necessarily from poor explanation.

items.example: The report's convoluted explanation obscured a simple result.
items.note: Criticises explanations or arguments that are unnecessarily intricate and hard to follow.

items.example: The athletes completed a gruelling training schedule before the event.
items.note: Stronger than arduous; highlights severe mental or physical exhaustion.

items.example: The constant interruptions made the meeting insufferable.
items.note: Strongly negative; especially used for people, behaviour, discomfort or extreme heat.

items.pt: obstrutivo; que cria obstáculos de propósito
items.example: The manager's obstructive behaviour delayed the safety review.
items.note: Often implies deliberately making cooperation or progress difficult.

items.example: It was a tough decision, but the team needed to abandon the old design.
items.note: Broad everyday adjective for situations, tasks or choices that demand resilience.

items.example: The traumatic experience affected her confidence for months.
items.note: Strongly distressing or shocking, rather than merely inconvenient or tiring.

items.example: The wayward apprentice repeatedly ignored the workshop rules.
items.note: Usually about people or behaviour that resists guidance and acts unpredictably.

items.example: We had difficulty reproducing the results on the second board.
items.note: Normally have difficulty (in) doing something: use singular difficulty in this construction.

items.example: Another compulsory registration form? What a pain!
items.note: Informal exclamation about something annoying or inconvenient.

items.example: The postponed concert was such a drag after months of planning.
items.note: Informal reaction to something tedious or disappointing.

items.example: Updating fifty separate spreadsheets became a real chore.
items.note: A boring task that has to be done; often in the phrase a real chore.

items.pt: o que deu nele?; o que o está incomodando?
items.example: He has been unusually rude all morning. What's eating him?
items.note: Informal question about why someone seems troubled or irritable.

items.example: He never raises his voice, so what's got into him today?
items.note: Informal way of expressing surprise at someone's unusual behaviour.

items.example: He seems distracted; do you know what's bugging him?
items.note: Informal: bug someone means bother or irritate them.

items.pt: o que está acontecendo com ele?; o que ele tem?
items.example: He keeps refusing to speak to anyone. What's up with him?
items.note: An informal question about another person's state or behaviour.

items.example: I chose the simpler setup to avoid the hassle of extra paperwork.
items.note: Informal noun for inconvenient trouble or needless difficulty.

items.example: Please don't hassle the technician for updates every ten minutes.
items.note: As a transitive verb, hassle someone means repeatedly bother or pressure them; distinct from the noun hassle.

items.example: Sitting through four hours of repetitive advertising was sheer torture.
items.note: Often deliberate exaggeration for an exceptionally unpleasant experience.

items.pt: dar o sangue; trabalhar até a exaustão
items.example: The volunteers slogged their guts out to finish the repairs on time.
items.note: Very informal, emphatic expression for working extremely hard.

items.example: She ground away at the calculations until the model finally converged.
items.note: Informal in this context: work persistently and laboriously, often grind away at something.

items.example: He grafted all summer to fund his postgraduate course.
items.note: Informal British English verb meaning work hard; not the medical or horticultural sense.

items.pt: matar-se de trabalhar; esforçar-se até a exaustão
items.example: You shouldn't flog yourself to death for a deadline that can be renegotiated.
items.note: Strong, informal exaggeration for overworking.

items.example: I'm in a fix because two essential appointments overlap.
items.note: Informal idiom for being in a difficult situation.

items.example: We were in a spot when the only working key went missing.
items.note: Informal; comparable to in a fix, sometimes a tight spot.

items.example: The team found itself in a hole after losing its main supplier.
items.note: Informal idiom for being trapped by a difficult situation.

items.pt: enfrentando grandes dificuldades; numa situação apertada
items.example: The small charity is really up against it after the funding cuts.
items.note: Informal expression for facing serious pressure or disadvantages.

items.example: I'm up to my neck in paperwork before the inspection.
items.note: Usually up to your neck in work, trouble or debt; indicates overwhelming involvement.

items.example: A confidential email sent to the wrong address created a sticky situation.
items.note: Informal: an awkward situation that is hard to resolve.

items.pt: situação complicada; situação difícil de resolver
items.example: The mediator handled a tricky situation between the two departments.
items.note: A problem needing tact or skill, not necessarily severe danger.

items.pt: livre de responsabilidade; fora de apuros
items.example: When the supplier accepted the fault, our team was off the hook.
items.note: Often means released from blame, responsibility or an unpleasant obligation.

items.pt: livre de suspeitas; fora de perigo ou problemas
items.example: Once the audit approved the accounts, the treasurer was in the clear.
items.note: No longer under suspicion or threat; precise meaning depends on context.

items.pt: fora de perigo; passado o pior
items.example: The patient is improving, but she isn't out of the woods yet.
items.note: Usually means the worst danger or difficulty has passed; often in negatives.

items.example: The main downside of the new sensor is its higher energy consumption.
items.note: A disadvantage or unfavourable aspect of an otherwise acceptable situation.

units.title: Unit 70 — Modality: expressing facts, opinions, desires
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 70. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Basic concepts · stance, probability, obligation and volition
learningObjectives: Express deductions, disbelief and speculative possibility with natural modal constructions.
Distinguish degrees of probability and certainty using bound to, odds, chances and likelihood.
Describe obligation and choice with essential, obligatory, compulsory, optional and no option but to.
Use formal and neutral expressions for determination, desire and aspiration with accurate complements.

sectionsChecked: D · Word families practised in exercises

items.example: I must admit that the original design was easier to maintain.
items.note: Conventional, measured admission; often prepares the listener for an honest opinion.

items.example: I must confess that I missed an important detail in the proposal.
items.note: Similar to must admit, but can suggest a more personal or reluctant disclosure.

items.example: I must say that the organisers handled the questions very well.
items.note: Introduces an emphatic personal evaluation; may praise or criticise.

items.pt: você só pode estar brincando; não pode ser sério
items.example: Another deadline tomorrow? You must be joking!
items.note: Strong reaction of disbelief, rather than a literal claim about comedy.

items.example: You must have been exhausted after the overnight journey.
items.note: Must have + past participle expresses a strong deduction about the past.

items.pt: é bem possível que; pode muito bem
items.example: The revised approach may well save the team several weeks.
items.note: Adds a substantial degree of plausibility without claiming certainty.

items.pt: é bem possível que; pode muito bem
items.example: If the tests pass, we might well finish ahead of schedule.
items.note: Tentative but plausible prediction; often slightly more cautious than may well.

items.pt: talvez nunca aconteça; pode ser que nem ocorra
items.example: Try not to worry about a possible inspection months in advance; it may never happen.
items.note: A reassuring, sometimes slightly dismissive phrase indicating that a feared event is uncertain.

items.example: What, may I ask, led you to reject the earlier findings?
items.note: A somewhat formal, occasionally pointed question formulation.

items.example: At the conference, who should I see but my former supervisor!
items.note: A literary or conversational construction expressing an unexpected encounter; followed by a person.
items.speechText: who should I see but Anna

items.example: There's no need to blame anyone for the broken glass; accidents will happen.
items.note: Fixed reassurance acknowledging that occasional mishaps are inevitable.

items.example: The van won't start even though its battery is fully charged.
items.note: Won't can express a machine's refusal or failure to work, not a human decision.

items.example: Someone is ringing the bell; that'll be the delivery driver.
items.note: Will can express a confident inference about a present situation.

items.pt: quem me dera; até parece que eu teria essa sorte
items.example: They might offer me a free upgrade, but I should be so lucky!
items.note: Usually humorous or sceptical: the speaker thinks that good outcome is very unlikely.

items.pt: é provável que; tudo indica que
items.example: The odds are that the committee will request another revision.
items.note: Predicts that something is likely, commonly followed by a that-clause.
items.speechText: the odds are that she'll win

items.pt: as chances são contrárias a; é improvável que
items.example: The odds are against our proposal receiving funding this year.
items.note: Highlights the low probability of success; against takes a noun or -ing phrase.

items.example: Without adequate testing, the change is bound to cause problems.
items.note: Be bound to + infinitive expresses strong expectation, not obligation here.

items.example: This is unquestionably the clearest explanation in the report.
items.note: Very strong adverb of certainty or endorsement.

items.example: It soon became apparent that the initial assumptions were wrong.
items.note: Apparent that means evident or clear; in other contexts apparent can mean seeming.

items.example: We cannot confirm the delivery date for sure yet.
items.note: Conversational expression of certainty, often placed near the end.

items.pt: muito provavelmente; ao que tudo indica
items.example: In all probability, the revised standard will be adopted next year.
items.note: A fairly formal way to express high probability, without complete certainty.

items.pt: é provável que; há boas chances de
items.example: The chances are that you'll need to recalibrate the equipment.
items.note: Informal to neutral prediction of a likely event.

items.example: There is every likelihood that the results will be published next month.
items.note: Normally there is every likelihood that + clause; signals strong probability.

items.example: In all likelihood, the policy change will take effect next semester.
items.note: A natural alternative to in all probability, explicitly practised in exercise 70.2.

items.example: It is essential that every participant receive clear instructions.
items.note: In formal requirements, it is essential that can take the base verb (subjunctive).

items.example: Protective clothing is obligatory inside the clean room.
items.note: Formal adjective stating a rule or requirement; near-synonym of compulsory.

items.pt: sem outra opção senão; não ter alternativa a não ser
items.example: When the road flooded, we had no option but to turn back.
items.note: Have no option but to + infinitive means no viable alternative.

items.example: The organisation has an obligation to protect confidential information.
items.note: Usually have an obligation to + infinitive; can express legal or moral duty.

items.example: The additional seminar is optional for experienced researchers.
items.note: Not required; contrasts with compulsory or obligatory.

items.example: Attendance at the induction session is compulsory.
items.note: Compulsory commonly describes institutional rules, subjects or attendance.

items.example: She is determined to complete the project despite the setbacks.
items.note: Be determined to + infinitive emphasises firm resolve.

items.example: The applicants were anxious to hear the panel's final decision.
items.note: Can express eager desire, sometimes with an undertone of worry.

items.example: The students are eager to contribute to the fieldwork.
items.note: Eager to + infinitive highlights strong positive willingness.

items.example: We are keen to establish a long-term research partnership.
items.note: Keen to + infinitive is common in British English; keen on + noun/-ing expresses interest.

items.example: After the review, the team was resolved to improve its procedures.
items.note: Formal synonym for determined; be resolved to + infinitive.

items.example: I wish to raise one additional point before the vote.
items.note: Wish to + infinitive is more formal than want to.

items.example: Several candidates desire a more flexible working arrangement.
items.note: Formal verb for a strong wish; can take a noun or to-infinitive.

items.example: After years away, he yearned to return to his hometown.
items.note: Strong, literary or formal desire; yearn to + infinitive or yearn for + noun.

items.example: After the exhausting shift, I longed to see my family.
items.note: Long to + infinitive / long for + noun is more everyday than yearn.

items.example: Her ambition is to establish an independent research group.
items.note: An important long-term aim, often ambition to + infinitive.

items.example: His aspiration is to work on sustainable energy systems.
items.note: Often an elevated or long-term personal goal; commonly plural aspirations.

items.section: D · Word families practised in exercises
items.example: Her determination kept the team focused during the crisis.
items.note: Noun from determine; often determination to + infinitive.

items.section: D · Word families practised in exercises
items.example: The novel captures the protagonist's yearning for home.
items.note: Noun from yearn; typically yearning for something or to do something.

items.section: D · Word families practised in exercises
items.example: He made a New Year's resolution to reduce his screen time.
items.note: Noun connected with resolve; a New Year's resolution is a firm self-promise.

items.section: D · Word families practised in exercises
items.example: The committee was desirous of reaching a fair settlement.
items.note: Markedly formal adjective; desirous of + noun/-ing, or desirous that + clause.

items.section: D · Word families practised in exercises
items.example: Her eagerness to learn impressed the visiting researchers.
items.note: Noun from eager; eagerness to + infinitive.

items.section: D · Word families practised in exercises
items.example: He spoke of his longing to see the coast again.
items.note: Noun from long; longing for + noun or longing to + infinitive.

items.section: D · Word families practised in exercises
items.example: It is an ambitious timetable for such a complex installation.
items.note: Can describe a person with strong goals or a plan that is difficult to achieve.
